spark.summary: Event-driven architecture (EDA) decouples producers and consumers by broadcasting immutable state-change facts through an asynchronous message broker or durable event log.
spark.keyTakeaway: Replacing synchronous RPC chains with durable partitioned logs (Kafka, Pulsar, Kinesis) isolates service failures and enables independent scaling—at the cost of eventual consistency and idempotency engineering.

concept.whyItMatters: In synchronous microservice chains (Order -> Inventory -> Payment -> Loyalty -> Email), end-to-end availability is the product of every downstream service's uptime, and a single slow dependency exhausts caller thread pools. Event-driven architecture breaks this temporal coupling: the Order service commits `OrderPlaced` to a durable log and returns immediately, while downstream consumers process the event at their own pace, replay history after bugs, or fan out to new features (fraud scoring, analytics) without modifying the producer.
whenToUse: Fan-out workflows where one domain action (e.g., `OrderPaid`) triggers 3+ independent side effects: inventory deduction, invoice PDF generation, analytics, and push notifications.
Traffic-spiky workloads (flash sales, market opens, IoT bursts) where a durable broker absorbs 10x–50x ingestion spikes so downstream databases don't melt.
Auditability and replayable state pipelines where multiple consumers need ordered, immutable change streams (CDC, event sourcing, real-time ML feature computation).
whenNotToUse: Strict synchronous request-response queries where the user needs an immediate, strongly consistent answer before proceeding (e.g., checking a live seat map or balance before debiting).
Simple 2-service CRUD apps where adding Kafka/ZooKeeper/Schema Registry introduces far more operational overhead than a direct HTTP call or Postgres job queue.
Distributed transactions requiring immediate two-phase commit (2PC) semantics across services that cannot tolerate eventual consistency windows.
keyPoints: Event vs. Command: An event (`OrderShipped`) is an immutable past-tense fact broadcast to unknown subscribers; a command (`ShipOrder`) is a directed imperative to one receiver.
Partitioned ordering: Logs like Apache Kafka guarantee strict FIFO ordering *within a single partition* (keyed by `order_id` or `tenant_id`), not globally across a topic.
Delivery semantics: Distributed brokers default to `at-least-once` delivery; consumers must be idempotent using deduplication keys (`event_id`) to achieve effectively `exactly-once` state.
Transactional Outbox: Never dual-write to Postgres and Kafka in the same request—write the event to an `outbox` table in the same ACID transaction and tail it via Debezium or a poller.
Consumer groups & backpressure: Independent consumer groups maintain their own offsets, allowing a slow analytics consumer to lag without blocking real-time fraud detection.

examples.title: Uber-Scale Ride Trip Lifecycle Fan-Out
examples.scenario: When a trip ends, the platform must calculate dynamic fare, charge the rider's card, update driver earnings, refresh surge-pricing heatmaps, and send a receipt. Synchronous HTTP calls caused cascading timeouts whenever the PDF receipt service degraded.
examples.outcome: Publishing a `TripCompleted` Protobuf event to Kafka keyed by `trip_id` isolated each domain into its own consumer group. Receipt-service outages now only increase consumer lag on that group while payments and driver payouts continue at p99 < 80 ms.

examples.title: Transactional Outbox for Ledger-to-Search Sync
examples.scenario: A fintech service updated a user's KYC status in PostgreSQL and then called `kafkaProducer.send()`. During network blips, Postgres committed while Kafka timed out—leaving search indices permanently stale for ~0.2% of updates.
examples.outcome: Inserting the event into a Postgres `outbox_events` table inside the same `BEGIN...COMMIT` transaction and streaming it via Debezium CDC eliminated dual-write drift completely (0 lost events over 18 months).

tradeOffs.pro: Producers stay fast and resilient even when downstream consumers are down for maintenance or deploying.
tradeOffs.con: Tracing a request across 6 async topics requires distributed tracing (`traceparent` headers in Kafka records) rather than a single call stack.

tradeOffs.pro: Eliminates distributed locks and 2PC bottlenecks, allowing each service to scale its own database independently.
tradeOffs.con: UI clients may read stale state for 50–500 ms after a write unless designed with optimistic UI updates or read-your-own-writes tokens.

tradeOffs.pro: A Schema Registry (Protobuf/Avro) lets producers and consumers evolve independently across deployments.
tradeOffs.con: Breaking field changes (renaming or changing types) require dual-publishing or versioned topics, slowing down rapid schema refactoring.

failureModes.name: Dual-Write Split-Brain
failureModes.description: Writing to the local DB and publishing to Kafka as two separate network calls causes silent divergence whenever one succeeds and the other crashes.
failureModes.mitigation: Use the Transactional Outbox pattern with Debezium CDC or a polling relay inside the same ACID database transaction.

failureModes.name: Poison-Pill Message Blocking a Partition
failureModes.description: A malformed or schema-incompatible message causes a consumer to crash in a tight loop; because offsets never advance, every healthy message behind it on that partition stalls indefinitely.
failureModes.mitigation: Route deserialization or permanent business errors to a Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ) after N bounded retries with exponential backoff.

failureModes.name: Hot-Partition Skew
failureModes.description: Keying a Kafka topic by `country_code` or a default `null` key routes 80% of traffic to a single partition, maxing out one consumer thread while 15 others sit idle.
failureModes.mitigation: Choose high-cardinality partition keys (`tenant_id` + `entity_id` or salted keys) and monitor per-partition lag.

failureModes.name: Consumer Rebalance Storms
failureModes.description: Long synchronous processing (> `max.poll.interval.ms`, default 5 min in Kafka) tricks the broker into thinking a consumer is dead, triggering stop-the-world rebalances and duplicate processing.
failureModes.mitigation: Keep poll batches small, offload heavy work to worker pools with `pause()`/`resume()`, and use CooperativeStickyAssignor.

commonMistakes: Publishing 'thin' events with only an ID (`OrderUpdated{id: 42}`) that force 10 consumers to DDoS the producer's REST API to fetch details—or 'fat' events that leak internal DB schemas.
Assuming global ordering across all partitions instead of keying related events (`order_id`) to the same partition.
Forgetting to make consumers idempotent, leading to double-charges or duplicate emails during consumer restarts or broker failover.
Using Kafka as a long-term random-access database without compaction or tiered storage governance.
Omitting `traceId` and `eventId` metadata headers, making incident root-cause analysis across async hops nearly impossible.

sections.content:
## The idea

Event-driven architecture shifts communication from **imperative point-to-point requests** ("Service A tells Service B what to do right now") to **asynchronous broadcast of state changes** ("Service A records that `OrderPaid` happened, and any interested service reacts").

Modern EDA centers on an **append-only, partitioned commit log** (Apache Kafka, Redpanda, AWS Kinesis) rather than ephemeral queues alone. Unlike traditional message queues (RabbitMQ) that delete a message once acknowledged, a log retains events for a configured retention window (e.g., 7 days or infinite compacted). Multiple independent consumer groups read from the same topic at their own offsets without interfering with one another.

## Concrete walkthrough

Walk through a resilient `OrderPlaced` flow using the **Transactional Outbox** and **Idempotent Consumers**:

1. **Atomic Write**: The Order service starts a Postgres transaction, inserts into `orders`, and inserts `{event_id: uuid, aggregate_id: 'ord-99', payload: ...}` into `outbox_events`, then commits.
2. **CDC Relay**: Debezium tails Postgres WAL and publishes the event to Kafka topic `orders.events` partitioned by `hash('ord-99') % 12`, ensuring all events for `ord-99` land on Partition 4 in exact order.
3. **Schema Validation**: The producer/relay validates the Avro/Protobuf payload against Confluent Schema Registry (`BACKWARD` compatibility).
4. **Consumer Processing**: The Inventory consumer group reads Partition 4, checks `processed_events(event_id)` in its own DB inside a single transaction, deducts stock, records `event_id`, and commits its Kafka offset.

sections.content:
## Delivery guarantees and idempotency

In distributed networks, **true exactly-once delivery across external side effects does not exist**—a consumer can apply a change and crash right before committing its offset. Therefore, systems target **at-least-once delivery + idempotent processing**:

- **Natural Idempotency**: Operations like `SET status = 'SHIPPED'` or `UPSERT` with a monotonic `version` timestamp (`WHERE incoming_version > current_version`) are safe to replay.
- **Deduplication Table**: For non-idempotent actions (incrementing a balance, sending an email), store `event_id` in a `processed_events` table with a `UNIQUE` constraint inside the same DB transaction as the state update.
- **Kafka Transactions (`read_committed`)**: Useful strictly for *Kafka-to-Kafka* stream processors (Kafka Streams, Flink) where inputs and outputs live inside the same cluster.

## Message broker & streaming comparison

| System | Storage Model | Ordering Scope | Replayability | Throughput / Latency | Ideal Use Case |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Apache Kafka / Redpanda** | Append-only partitioned log | Per-partition | Full (days to infinite) | 1M+ msg/s, 2–15 ms | Event streaming, CDC, multi-consumer fan-out |
| **RabbitMQ (Classic/Quorum)** | Smart broker / ephemeral queue | Per-queue (single consumer) | No (deleted on ACK) | 50k–100k msg/s, <5 ms | Complex routing, task queues, RPC replies |
| **AWS SQS + SNS** | Managed queue + pub/sub | Best-effort (FIFO: per-group) | No (DLQ only) | Elastic (FIFO: 3k–70k/s) | Serverless AWS fan-out with zero ops |
| **Apache Pulsar** | Segmented log (BookKeeper) | Per-partition / Key_Shared | Full (tiered storage) | 1M+ msg/s, 5–15 ms | Multi-tenant streaming + queue semantics |

## Failure modes

- **Unbounded Consumer Lag**: A slow downstream DB causes consumer lag to grow from 100 to 50M messages. Once lag exceeds the broker's retention period (e.g., 7 days), unconsumed events are permanently deleted before being read.
- **Out-of-Order Retries**: Retrying a failed message by re-publishing it to the *end* of a topic breaks per-key ordering (`OrderCancelled` processed before `OrderCreated`). Use version checks or per-key retry queues.
- **Schema Compatibility Breakage**: Removing a required field without bumping the major version crashes every downstream consumer simultaneously.

## Choreography vs. orchestration

As event-driven workflows grow past 4–5 steps, pure **choreography** (services reacting to each other's events without a central coordinator) becomes hard to reason about—no single place shows whether a saga succeeded or stalled.

- Use **Choreography** for independent, decoupled side effects (analytics, search indexing, notifications).
- Use **Orchestration** (Temporal, AWS Step Functions, or a dedicated Saga Coordinator) when a multi-step business transaction requires strict sequencing, timeouts, and compensating rollbacks (e.g., reserve flight -> reserve hotel -> charge card -> rollback flight on hotel failure).

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Use the Transactional Outbox pattern (or native CDC) instead of dual-writing to a database and a broker.
- [ ] Partition topics by entity/aggregate ID (`order_id`, `account_id`) to preserve causal ordering without hot-spotting.
- [ ] Enforce schema contracts (`BACKWARD` or `FULL` compatibility) via Schema Registry in CI/CD.
- [ ] Make every consumer idempotent via `event_id` deduplication or monotonic `version` guards.
- [ ] Configure bounded retries and a Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ) with alerting and a replay runbook.
- [ ] Propagate W3C `traceparent` and `correlation_id` in event headers and alert on `consumer_lag` before retention expiry.

questions.title: Message Ordering in Distributed Log Partitions
questions.prompt: How does Apache Kafka guarantee strict sequential ordering for messages delivered to consumers?

options.text: It uses a single global lock across all cluster brokers.
options.explanation: Global locks destroy distributed log throughput.

options.text: It routes messages with the same partition key to a single partition, where they are appended sequentially to a single log.
options.explanation: Correct! Sequential ordering is guaranteed per partition key.

rubric.excellent: Explains partition keys and single-partition log append ordering.
rubric.gap: Thinks global ordering across all partitions is default.

questions.sampleSolution: Kafka guarantees message order within a single partition by routing messages with identical partition keys to that partition.
questions.explanation: Per-partition sequential log appends preserve order without bottlenecking the entire cluster.

interviewProblems.title: Reliable E-Commerce Order Processing Pipeline
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: You are designing the order processing backend for an e-commerce platform during Black Friday. When a customer places an order, 5 downstream services (Inventory, Billing, Shipping, Analytics, Fraud) must process it. How do you ensure high throughput and zero lost orders if Shipping goes down?

dimensions.name: Asynchronous Decoupling
dimensions.description: Publishing OrderPlaced events to Kafka topic instead of blocking HTTP.

dimensions.name: Idempotency & Retry Safety
dimensions.description: Handling duplicate message delivery using idempotent consumer keys.

interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Publish OrderPlaced events to a durable Kafka topic with 7-day retention. Each downstream service consumes from its own consumer group. If Shipping fails, its consumer offset pauses while other services continue unimpeded.
commonPitfalls: Chaining synchronous HTTP calls from Payment -> Inventory -> Shipping.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Event-driven architecture (EDA) decouples producers and consumers by broadcasting immutable state-change facts through an asynchronous message broker or durable event log.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Inventory Consumer applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Dead-Letter Topic.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Dead-Letter Topic experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Use the Transactional Outbox pattern with Debezium CDC or a polling relay inside the same ACID database transaction.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Replacing synchronous RPC chains with durable partitioned logs (Kafka, Pulsar, Kinesis) isolates service failures and enables independent scaling—at the cost of eventual consistency and idempotency engineering.
Avoid trap: Publishing 'thin' events with only an ID (`OrderUpdated{id: 42}`) that force 10 consumers to DDoS the producer's REST API to fetch details—or 'fat' events that leak internal DB schemas.
Avoid trap: Assuming global ordering across all partitions instead of keying related events (`order_id`) to the same partition.

When to reach for it: Fan-out workflows where one domain action (e.g., `OrderPaid`) triggers 3+ independent side effects: inventory deduction, invoice PDF generation, analytics, and push notifications.
When to reach for it: Traffic-spiky workloads (flash sales, market opens, IoT bursts) where a durable broker absorbs 10x–50x ingestion spikes so downstream databases don't melt.

putItTogether.title: Putting Event Driven Architecture Together
putItTogether.summary: Replacing synchronous RPC chains with durable partitioned logs (Kafka, Pulsar, Kinesis) isolates service failures and enables independent scaling—at the cost of eventual consistency and idempotency engineering.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Event Driven Architecture before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Publishing a `TripCompleted` Protobuf event to Kafka keyed by `trip_id` isolated each domain into its own consumer group. Receipt-service outages now only increase consumer lag on that group while payments and driver payouts continue at p99 < 80 ms.
